## Montezuma: A Picturesque Village in Costa Rica

Montezuma attracts ecotourists, beach lovers and admirers of extraordinary natural beauty. The small village's beach is surrounded by high cliffs covered in tropical vegetation, picturesque waterfalls and natural pools.

The center of Montezuma, with its old wooden houses, draws wandering artists. An open-air bar with a dance floor opens onto a street overlooking the ocean, where romantics can watch the moon and the shimmering waters of the Gulf of Nicoya.

## Cloud Forest and the Quetzal: What to See in Monteverde, Costa Rica

Monteverde was founded by Quakers as a center for one branch of Protestantism. It is a very welcoming and charming place. Surrounded by lush greenery, the small town is ideal for walks, after which you can relax in a small café with fragrant coffee or freshly squeezed tropical fruit juice.

## Monteverde Cloud Forest

You can take a tour of the biological reserve of tropical birds and may even spot the rare quetzal. An excursion to the butterfly reserve and the songbird gallery is also particularly interesting. The Monteverde Reserve <>, established in 1972, is one of the best-known reserves in the world and one of Costa Rica's most important private protected areas, covering 3,500 hectares. In 2007, it was chosen as one of the Seven Wonders of Costa Rica.

Monteverde's forests contain four ecological "life zones" with distinct ecosystems. They are home to hundreds of species of mammals, birds, butterflies, amphibians, reptiles, insects and spiders, as well as diverse mosses, epiphytes, vines and other plants and trees typical of cloud forests.

Montevideo's Metropolitan Cathedral stands in the historic part of Uruguay's capital. Its pale facade with two towers faces a city square, and its restrained proportions reflect neoclassical architecture.

Construction of the present church began in 1790, and it was consecrated in 1804. In 1897, it gained cathedral status. A visit offers an introduction to Montevideo's religious history and complements a walk through the old town.

Independence Square marks the transition between Montevideo's historic neighborhoods and its newer streets. An equestrian monument to José Artigas rises at its center, while the Gateway of the Citadel survives on the western side.

The square became one of the capital's main public spaces after the city expanded beyond its colonial fortifications. From here, it is easy to continue walking along the pedestrian streets of Ciudad Vieja and admire the buildings surrounding the square.

Montevideo's old town is known as Ciudad Vieja. This was once a fortified colonial city, and the surviving Gateway of the Citadel marks the passage from Independence Square into its historic streets.

As you explore, you will see historic houses, museums, cafés, bookstores and antique shops. The pedestrian Sarandí Street leads deeper into the neighborhood. The old town is easy to explore together with the cathedral and the capital's squares.
